items.title: [nltk] NLTK: BllipParser passes caller-supplied model paths to the bllipparser C extension with no pathsec check, enabling arbitrary read
items.summary: SummaryBllipParser in nltk/parse/bllip.py hands caller-supplied filesystem paths to the native bllipparser C extension without routing them through NLTK's pathsec validation. The constructor parameters parser_model, reranker_features, and reranker_weights, and the alternative from_unified_model_dir() entry point, flow directly to the C extension's load_parser_model() and load_reranker_model() calls, which open and read the given path at the OS level. Any application that passes an attacker-influenced path to this API reads a file of the attacker's choosing from anywhere on the filesystem, outside the NLTK data roots that every other NLTK tool wrapper confines access to.Root CauseAs of NLTK 3.10.0, SECURITY.md documents a centralized I/O security module (nltk.pathsec) with strict enforcement enabled by default, under which file-backed resources must resolve inside allowed NLTK data directories. For paths handed to external tools and native extensions that open files themselves, the module provides validate_tool_path(), which runs name-safety checks, rejects option-shaped, URL-shaped, and traversal inputs, opens the path with O_NOFOLLOW requiring a regular single-linked file, and returns the validated string the caller must use. Every sibling tool wrapper applies it. BllipParser applies none of it: the module imports only ParserI, safe_print, and Tree, with zero pathsec references, so the three model-path parameters reach the C extension unchecked. The violated invariant is that NLTK tool wrappers must bound caller-supplied native-tool paths to the data roots before the native code opens them.nltk/parse/bllip.py:125-131   BllipParser.__init__ accepts parser_model,                              reranker_features, reranker_weights (no validation)nltk/parse/bllip.py:164       self.rrp.load_parser_model(parser_model, ...)   -> C extension opennltk/parse/bllip.py:166-170   self.rrp.load_reranker_model(features_filename=...,                              weights_filename=...)                          -> C extension opennltk/parse/bllip.py:218-255   from_unified_model_dir(model_dir) -> __init__ (no validation)nltk/parse/bllip.py:9-11      imports: ParserI, safe_print, Tree (no pathsec import)ImpactAn application that uses BllipParser (requiring the optional bllipparser package to be installed) and that passes a model path derived from untrusted input to the constructor or to from_unified_model_dir() allows that input to designate an arbitrary filesystem path. The native extension opens and reads the designated file into process memory to parse it as model data. This defeats the pathsec data-root confinement that NLTK applies to all other native-tool model loads. The attacker-controlled path can target files outside the NLTK data directories, for example local configuration or credential files readable by the process. Content disclosure to the attacker depends on how the application surfaces parser errors or results; file existence, size, and open behavior provide an oracle regardless. Because the same unvalidated path also skips the checks that refuse a non-regular file or an over-large model, the attacker can instead designate a FIFO, socket, device, or directory, or an oversized regular file, so the native load blocks or reads unbounded data into memory and the component performing the parse suffers reduced performance or a stalled worker. The primitive demonstrated by source analysis is attacker control of which file the process opens and reads.Proof of ConceptRequires the optional bllipparser C extension to be installed(pip install bllipparser) so that RerankingParser.load_parser_modelis available. No NLTK data download is needed to exercise the path.# An application forwards an untrusted "model" path into BllipParser.from nltk.parse.bllip import BllipParser# Attacker-controlled value reaches the constructor unchanged.untrusted_path = "/etc/passwd"BllipParser(parser_model=untrusted_path)# The bllipparser C extension opens and reads untrusted_path at the OS# level with no NLTK pathsec confinement to the data roots.Structural confirmation without the optional extension installed:$ grep -n "pathsec\|validate_path\|validate_tool" nltk/parse/bllip.py(no output)$ grep -n "validate_tool_path" nltk/tag/crf.py nltk/tag/hunpos.py \      nltk/tag/stanford.py nltk/parse/malt.pynltk/tag/crf.py:140nltk/tag/crf.py:311nltk/tag/hunpos.py:111nltk/tag/stanford.py:85nltk/tag/stanford.py:137nltk/parse/malt.py:340nltk/parse/malt.py:344BllipParser is the only native-tool wrapper with no validate_tool_path call.Attack ChainExposure: An application imports BllipParser (exported at nltk/parse/bllip.py:83 and re-exported at nltk/parse/__init__.py:47) and constructs it with a model path influenced by untrusted input.Control: The attacker controls the parser_model, reranker_features, or reranker_weights string (or the model_dir passed to from_unified_model_dir() at nltk/parse/bllip.py:218); it is accepted as an arbitrary string with no type o

items.title: [nltk] NLTK: Quadratic CPU exhaustion in LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize via unguarded onset reversal loop
items.summary: SummaryLegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize in the NLTK tokenizer package contains an unguarded O(n^2) processing loop. When the method is called on a single token that consists of a long run of vowels (for example "a" * n), it consumes CPU time proportional to the square of the token length. An attacker who can supply an untrusted token to this public tokenizer API can force a single request to saturate one CPU core for a prolonged period, degrading availability of any service that syllabifies attacker-controlled text. No authentication, special configuration, or user interaction is required.Root CauseThe method walks the token in reverse and, on every iteration after the first vowel is seen, evaluates the membership test char_lower + current_onset[::-1] in self.legal_onsets. The set legal_onsets is built by onset(), which returns only the characters up to the first vowel, so every member is vowel-free. For an all-vowel token the first branch can therefore never match, onset never becomes True, and the reset branch that would clear current_onset is never reached. As a result current_onset grows by one character on every iteration. Building current_onset[::-1] and hashing the resulting string costs O(k) on iteration k, and this is repeated for k from 1 to n, giving total cost O(n^2). The security invariant that is violated is bounded per-token work: there is no length cap on this code path, so untrusted token length translates directly into quadratic CPU consumption.Affected function: LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenizeSource: nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py (membership-test sink at line 133; loop over token[::-1] beginning at line 126)Helper establishing the vowel-free onset set: LegalitySyllableTokenizer.onset (nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py, returns prefix up to first vowel)ImpactAn attacker who controls a token passed to LegalitySyllableTokenizer.tokenize can trigger quadratic CPU work. In the reviewed release a token of roughly 64,000 vowel characters takes about 1.8 seconds on a single core, and the cost grows with the square of the length, so a token in the hundreds of kilobytes to megabyte range consumes a core for many seconds to minutes. Memory use is linear. The demonstrated capability is single-core CPU exhaustion leading to denial of service or latency degradation in any network-reachable component that syllabifies untrusted input. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact; the effect is availability degradation of the affected process. The plausible operational consequence, where multiple concurrent requests are used, is exhaustion of the available worker pool; this is inferred from the per-request cost and was not itself executed against a live deployment.Proof of ConceptRequires only the released nltk package; no corpus download is needed because the quadratic behavior is driven entirely by the attacker token, not by the size of the legal-onset set.Construct a tokenizer with any small onset source.Call tokenize with an all-vowel token of increasing length and time each call.Compare against a consonant-alternating control token of equal length.import timefrom nltk.tokenize import LegalitySyllableTokenizertok = LegalitySyllableTokenizer("tr c d".split())  # tiny 3-word onset sourcefor n in (8000, 16000, 32000):    payload = "a" * n    start = time.perf_counter()    tok.tokenize(payload)    print("vowel-run", n, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3))control = "ba" * 32000  # equal-length linear controlstart = time.perf_counter()tok.tokenize(control)print("control", 64000, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3))vowel-run 8000 0.031vowel-run 16000 0.120vowel-run 32000 0.468   (about 4x per doubling => O(n^2))control 64000 0.004     (linear, roughly 130x faster at larger size)Attack ChainExposure: LegalitySyllableTokenizer is exported from nltk.tokenize and tokenize is a public, documented method reachable by any service that syllabifies untrusted text.Control: The attacker fully controls the token argument, including its length and character content; a run of vowels such as "a" * n survives with no normalization or length reduction.Path: The token flows into the reverse walk at nltk/tokenize/legality_principle.py:126 and reaches the membership-test at line 133 on every iteration past the first vowel.Guard: There is no length cap on this path. The sibling SyllableTokenizer received a MAX_TOKEN_LEN cap during the project hardening work, but legality_principle.py received no such guard.Primitive: Repeated O(k) construction and hashing of current_onset[::-1] inside the loop yields cumulative O(n^2) CPU work.Result: A single request with a large vowel-run token exhausts one CPU core for a sustained period, degrading service availability.Bypass EvidenceNo guard blocks this path. Membership-set analysis shows the first branch at line 133 cannot fire for a vowel character because legal_onsets is provably vowel-free (it is derived from onset(), which stops at the first vowel), so onset never be

items.title: [nltk] NLTK: Quadratic CPU exhaustion in TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize via list.pop(0) in quote-restore loop
items.summary: SummaryTreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize in the NLTK tokenizer package contains an unguarded O(n^2) processing loop in its quote-restoration step. When the method is invoked on text containing a long run of double-quote characters (for example '"' * n), it performs a list.pop(0) operation once per quote token, and because list.pop(0) is O(length), the total cost grows with the square of the input length. An attacker who can supply untrusted text to this public span-tokenization API can force a single request to saturate one CPU core for a prolonged period, degrading availability. No authentication, special configuration, or user interaction is required.Root CauseInside span_tokenize, when the input contains double or repeated quotes, the code builds matched, a list with one entry per quote occurrence, and then reconstructs tokens in a comprehension that calls matched.pop(0) for each token that is a quote. Removing the first element of a Python list is an O(len(list)) operation because all remaining elements are shifted. For an all-quote input the tokenizer produces n quote tokens and matched has n entries, so pop(0) is called n times, each time on a list of shrinking but still linear length, giving cumulative O(n^2) CPU work. The violated invariant is bounded per-input work: there is no length cap on span_tokenize or the underlying tokenize, so untrusted input length translates into quadratic processing time. The neighboring align_tokens call is linear and is not the quadratic term.Affected function: TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenizeSource: nltk/tokenize/treebank.py  - branch selector at line 203  - matched list built at line 205  - quadratic sink matched.pop(0) at line 209  - linear align_tokens call at line 215ImpactAn attacker who controls text passed to TreebankWordTokenizer.span_tokenize can trigger quadratic CPU work. In the reviewed release, an all-quote input of 128,000 characters takes about 1.76 seconds and 256,000 characters about 6.57 seconds on a single core, with cost growing as the square of the length. Memory use is linear. The demonstrated capability is single-core CPU exhaustion producing denial of service or latency degradation in any network-reachable component that uses span tokenization on untrusted input, such as offset, annotation, or highlighting pipelines. There is no confidentiality or integrity impact. The plausible operational consequence, where multiple concurrent requests are used, is worker-pool exhaustion; this is inferred from the measured per-request cost and was not executed against a live deployment.Proof of ConceptRequires only the released nltk package; no corpus download is needed.Instantiate TreebankWordTokenizer.Call span_tokenize on an all-double-quote string of increasing length and time each call.Compare against an equal-token-count control input that avoids the quote branch.import timefrom nltk.tokenize import TreebankWordTokenizertok = TreebankWordTokenizer()for n in (32000, 64000, 128000, 256000):    payload = '"' * n    start = time.perf_counter()    list(tok.span_tokenize(payload))    print("quote-run", n, round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3))control = "a " * 128000  # comparable token count, avoids the pop(0) branchstart = time.perf_counter()list(tok.span_tokenize(control))print("control", round(time.perf_counter() - start, 3))quote-run 32000 0.23quote-run 64000 0.52quote-run 128000 1.76quote-run 256000 6.57   (about 4x per doubling => O(n^2))control 0.16            (roughly 11x faster, isolates pop(0))Attack ChainExposure: TreebankWordTokenizer is exported from nltk.tokenize and span_tokenize is a public, documented method reachable by any service that span-tokenizes untrusted text.Control: The attacker fully controls the text argument; a run of double-quote characters such as '"' * n survives to the quote branch unchanged.Path: The branch selector at line 203 ('"' in text or "''" in text) is satisfied by the payload, entering the vulnerable branch; matched is built at line 205 with n entries and the reconstruction comprehension runs at line 209.Guard: There is no length cap on span_tokenize or tokenize. The regex timeout backstop in nltk/redos.py only wraps regular-expression operations and does not cover the pure-Python list.pop(0) sink; a 256,000-character input ran to completion in 6.57 seconds with no timeout raised.Primitive: matched.pop(0) executed once per quote token, each call O(len(matched)), yields cumulative O(n^2) CPU work.Result: A single request with a large quote-run input exhausts one CPU core for a sustained period, degrading service availability.Bypass EvidenceNo guard blocks this path. Direct inspection found no MAX_TOKEN_LEN or length check in nltk/tokenize/treebank.py, in contrast to the sibling sonority_sequencing.py which does cap token length. items.title: [nltk] NLTK: Unbounded CPU consumption in SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.parse() with ambiguous or self-embedding grammars
items.summary: Summarynltk.parse.recursivedescent.SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.parse() performs an unbounded top-down search over ambiguous or self-embedding context-free grammars with no wall-clock or step limit. An actor who can influence the grammar and supply a short input to a caller that uses this parser can force a single parse() call to pin a CPU core indefinitely, producing a denial of service. The related base class RecursiveDescentParser gained a max_time wall-clock deadline, but the stepping subclass drives its own step loop and never arms or consults that deadline, and its constructor does not accept a max_time parameter, so the guard cannot be enabled on this path.Root CauseRecursiveDescentParser bounds its recursive search inside _parse: it arms a wall-clock deadline on the first step and raises TimeoutError once max_time (default 5.0 seconds) is exceeded. SteppingRecursiveDescentParser was designed for interactive single-stepping and overrides both parse() and _parse. Its parse() runs initialize() followed by a while self.step() is not None loop that never enters the guarded base _parse. Its _parse override is a state-capturing stub that records history and returns a sentinel, and it never references the inherited self._parse_deadline or self._max_time. Its __init__ signature omits max_time entirely, so a caller cannot enable or tighten a bound. The security invariant that a single parse must terminate within a bounded time is therefore never enforced on this parser.Affected component: nltk.parse.recursivedescent.SteppingRecursiveDescentParser- parse()      nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:428-433  (drives its own step loop, no bound armed or checked)- _parse()     nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:643-668  (stub override; never consults self._parse_deadline / self._max_time)- __init__()   nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:410-418  (signature (self, grammar, trace=0); no max_time parameter)Base guard for comparison: RecursiveDescentParser._parse nltk/parse/recursivedescent.py:141-150ImpactAn actor who controls or influences the grammar passed to SteppingRecursiveDescentParser and can supply a short token sequence to a caller that invokes parse() can cause that call to never return. The top-down search enumerates a derivation space that grows on the order of the Catalan numbers with no memoization of the search and no deadline, so one crafted grammar plus a short input deterministically consumes a CPU core. In a deployment that parses attacker-influenced input on a bounded worker pool, repeated requests exhaust the pool and deny service to legitimate users. No authentication, privilege, or user interaction is required in that worst-credible deployment. Exploitation requires that the target actually use this parser on untrusted input; because the stepping parser is primarily a debugging or interactive-stepping component that backs a GUI, real-world exposure is narrower than for the base parser, though parse() is a supported public method that behaves as a full parser.Proof of ConceptRequires only the nltk package (3.10.3) and standard library; no data downloads or network access.Reproduction steps:Build an ambiguous, self-embedding grammar such as S -> 'a' S S | 'a'.Confirm the base parser self-terminates: RecursiveDescentParser(g, max_time=2.0).parse(['a']*17) raises TimeoutError at about 2 seconds.Run the stepping parser on the same grammar and input and observe it never returns.import time, inspectfrom nltk import CFGfrom nltk.parse.recursivedescent import RecursiveDescentParser, SteppingRecursiveDescentParserg = CFG.fromstring("S -> 'a' S S | 'a'")# Base parser is bounded and self-terminates.try:    list(RecursiveDescentParser(g, max_time=2.0).parse(['a'] * 17))except TimeoutError:    print("base: TimeoutError (guarded)")# Stepping subclass cannot be bounded: no max_time parameter.print("stepping __init__ sig:", inspect.signature(SteppingRecursiveDescentParser.__init__))# Stepping parser runs unbounded on the same input.t0 = time.perf_counter()list(SteppingRecursiveDescentParser(g).parse(['a'] * 17))  # does not returnprint("stepping: returned after", time.perf_counter() - t0)base: TimeoutError (guarded)stepping __init__ sig: (self, grammar, trace=0)# stepping len3: 1 parse in 0.001s ; len7: 5 in 0.017s ; len9: 14 in 0.075s ; len11: 42 in 0.36s# stepping len17: still running past a 10s watchdog, process alive, no RecursionErrorAttack ChainExposure: A caller uses nltk.parse.SteppingRecursiveDescentParser, a public exported symbol (nltk/parse/__init__.py:97), invoking parse(tokens) on grammar and input influenced by an actor.Control: The actor influences the grammar (an ambiguous, self-embedding CFG such as S -> 'a' S S | 'a') and supplies a short token list (for example 17 copies of 'a'). Both survive to the parser unchanged.Path: parse() (recursivedescent.py:428) calls initialize() then loops while self.step() is not None; step() (:479) calls match()/expand() (:552/:512) which call the inherited _match/_expand

items.title: [nltk] NLTK: Symlink escape in YCOECorpusReader lets a psd/pos directory symlink read files outside the corpus root within the data sandbox
items.summary: SummaryYCOECorpusReader builds two nested corpus sub-readers whose roots are derived from self.root.join("psd") and self.root.join("pos") (nltk/corpus/reader/ycoe.py). Because FileSystemPathPointer.join() (nltk/data.py) performs a purely lexical containment check and never resolves symlinks, and because CorpusReader.__init__ (nltk/corpus/reader/api.py) validates a sub-reader root only against the global NLTK data sandbox and not against the enclosing corpus root, a directory symlink named psd or pos planted inside a YCOE corpus lets the reader anchor its nested sub-readers outside the YCOE corpus root. An attacker who controls the contents of a YCOE corpus loaded under pathsec.ENFORCE=True can make parsed_sents(), tagged_words(), and related methods return file content from other locations inside the allowed data sandbox, defeating the per-corpus-root containment boundary the pathsec controls are meant to enforce.Root CauseNLTK's pathsec controls are designed to keep each corpus reader confined to its own corpus root. The scoped containment is enforced through validate_path(..., required_root=self._root) at read time. However, the containment invariant is violated at reader-construction time for nested readers:FileSystemPathPointer.join() accepts a component that is a directory symlink because it only checks the joined string lexically (os.path.normpath plus a startswith prefix test) and never calls resolve().CorpusReader.__init__ validates the resulting sub-reader root string, but calls validate_path without required_root, so only the global-sandbox layer runs; the scoped per-corpus-root layer is skipped. The symlink is resolved by that global check, its target is found to be inside the allowed sandbox, and the sub-reader is accepted with its root pointing at the escaped target.From that point every read the sub-reader performs is scoped to the already-escaped root, so no later guard re-anchors it to the YCOE corpus root.Affected functions:- nltk.corpus.reader.ycoe.YCOECorpusReader.__init__   (nltk/corpus/reader/ycoe.py) builds nested sub-readers from self.root.join("psd")/("pos") without containing them to the parent root- nltk.corpus.reader.api.CorpusReader.__init__        (nltk/corpus/reader/api.py) validates a sub-reader root only against the global sandbox (validate_path without required_root)- nltk.data.FileSystemPathPointer.join               (nltk/data.py) applies a lexical prefix check only and never resolves symlinksImpactAn attacker who controls the directory contents of a YCOE corpus that is loaded by a victim application under pathsec.ENFORCE=True (the default in the affected releases) can read file content that lives outside the YCOE corpus root but inside an allowed NLTK data root. The disclosure is bounded to the global NLTK data sandbox: a symlink whose target resolves outside every allowed root is rejected at construction, so this is not an arbitrary-filesystem read. The demonstrated capability is read-only cross-corpus-root disclosure. In a multi-tenant or automated-ingestion deployment the accessible scope includes other corpora placed under the shared data path and the shared system temporary directory, which is a default allowed root and can hold other processes' sensitive temporary files. There is no integrity or availability impact.Proof of ConceptDependencies: a released nltk (3.10.0 through 3.10.3) on a POSIX host. No third-party packages. The only allowed data root is a fresh temp sandbox; ENFORCE is left at its default of True.Steps:Create a sandbox directory and register it as the sole nltk.data.path entry.Inside the sandbox create a "victim" directory holding doc1.psd / doc1.pos outside the YCOE corpus root.Create a YCOE corpus root whose psd and pos entries are directory symlinks pointing at the victim directory.Construct YCOECorpusReader on that root and read it.import os, tempfile, nltkfrom nltk import pathsecsandbox = os.path.realpath(tempfile.mkdtemp())pathsec.ENFORCE = Truenltk.data.path = [sandbox]pathsec._ALLOWED_ROOTS_CACHE = Nonefrom nltk.corpus.reader.ycoe import YCOECorpusReadervictim = os.path.join(sandbox, "victim", "psd_secret")victim_pos = os.path.join(sandbox, "victim", "pos_secret")os.makedirs(victim); os.makedirs(victim_pos)open(os.path.join(victim, "doc1.psd"), "w").write("(S (SECRET leaked-out-of-ycoe-root))\n")open(os.path.join(victim_pos, "doc1.pos"), "w").write("SECRET_NN leaked-out-of-ycoe-root_NN\n")ycoe = os.path.join(sandbox, "corpora", "ycoe_evil"); os.makedirs(ycoe)os.symlink(victim, os.path.join(ycoe, "psd"))os.symlink(victim_pos, os.path.join(ycoe, "pos"))reader = YCOECorpusReader(ycoe)print(reader.parsed_sents())print(reader.tagged_words())psd sub-reader real root : /tmp/ycoe_poc_zc35zihw/victim/psd_secretycoe corpus root         : /tmp/ycoe_poc_zc35zihw/corpora/ycoe_evilparsed_sents()           : [Tree('S', [Tree('SECRET', ['leaked-out-of-ycoe-root'])])]tagged_words()           : [('SECRET', 'NN'), ('leaked-out-of-ycoe-root', 'NN')]ESCAPE CONF

items.title: [nltk] Duplicate Advisory: Symlink escape in YCOECorpusReader lets a psd/pos directory symlink read files outside the corpus root within the data sandbox
items.summary: Duplicate AdvisoryThis advisory has been withdrawn because it is a duplicate of GHSA-qg35-44qx-7vrr. This link is maintained to preserve external references.Original DescriptionNLTK from 3.10.0 before 3.10.4 contains a symlink escape vulnerability in YCOECorpusReader that allows attackers to read files outside the corpus root by planting psd or pos directory symlinks. Attackers controlling a YCOE corpus can make parsed_sents() and tagged_words() return file content from other corpora or temporary files within the NLTK data sandbox.Referenceshttps://github.com/nltk/nltk/security/advisories/GHSA-qg35-44qx-7vrrhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-126304https://www.vulncheck.com/advisories/nltk-3.10.0-before-3.10.4-symlink-escape-in-ycoecorpusreaderhttps://github.com/advisories/GHSA-7r4r-6ppg-7ff8

items.title: [tornado] Tornado: Open redirect via triple-slash redirect paths
items.summary: SummaryDue to differences in the way browsers and Python's urllib parse urls, browsers treat a string starting with three or more slashes as a protocol-level redirect, while urllib does not. This means that the 6.6.0 fix for the RedirectHandler open redirect (CVE-2026-116578, commit cc75ab0e) is incomplete. Tornado 6.6.1 improves the open-redirect detection to handle this case correctly, as well as fixing a regression in the 6.6.0 implementation.Referenceshttps://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/security/advisories/GHSA-5cjw-f85j-cv6rhttps://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-126347https://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/commit/c503241622c0efe7c40110d89834ce8b7fead1e4https://github.com/tornadoweb/tornado/releases/tag/v6.6.1https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-5cjw-f85j-cv6r

items.title: [dnspython] dnspython has excessive memory and CPU use
items.summary: SummaryA maliciously crafted zone file could use a WKS record to consume excessive memory and CPU, possibly causing the process to exit due to memory exhaustion.DetailsThe from_text() parser does not check that a WKS record service number is between 0 and 65535 inclusive.  It then uses this number to resize the bitmap to accommodate a bit with that offset.  This can cause extremely large memory allocations, and also extends the array very inefficiently, wasting CPU.Proof of conceptThis demonstrates the failure to limit the service number, though with a value that does not cause excessive memory or CPU consumption.rd = dns.rdata.from_text("IN", "WKS", "10.0.0.1 udp 65536")ImpactIf dnspython is used to read zonefile format where the attacker can control the type and rdata text, the program may consume excessive memory or CPU, denying service.Referenceshttps://github.com/rthalley/dnspython/security/advisories/GHSA-vvf4-9x63-8xvvhttps://github.com/rthalley/dnspython/commit/388db14ee9923288f6e73f86e482c77706e59d73https://github.com/rthalley/dnspython/commit/a62e1be066da0ed71b5b59f37435bb17cfa0070fhttps://github.com/rthalley/dnspython/releases/tag/v2.9.2https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-vvf4-9x63-8xvv
